mainTopic: Saying both 'ratified' (קיום) and 'nullified' (הפרה) about a vow, and saying 'ratified for you today'
overview: This amud continues רבה's questions about a husband or father who speaks about a vow using both הקמה (ratifying) and הפרה (nullifying). First the גמרא answers an earlier question from the מחלוקת of רבי מאיר and רבי יוסי about a person who names an animal as a תמורה for both an עולה and a שלמים. Then it adds that when the husband openly makes the הקמה depend on the הפרה, even רבי מאיר agrees the הפרה works. Next רבה asks what happens if he says 'ratified and nullified' at the very same moment. The גמרא answers from רבה's own rule: what cannot work one after the other cannot work at the same time either. Finally רבה asks a new question: does 'ratified for you today' quietly mean 'nullified tomorrow'? That question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Proof from the dispute about a double substitute
steps.stepSummary: To answer רבה's earlier question, the גמרא brings the מחלוקת of רבי מאיר and רבי יוסי about someone who names an animal as a substitute for two different offerings.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear an answer from the dispute between רבי מאיר and רבי יוסי. We learned: if someone says about an animal 'This is a substitute for an עולה, a substitute for a שלמים,' it becomes a substitute only for the עולה. That is רבי מאיר's view. רבי יוסי says: if he meant both from the start, then since nobody can say two names at the exact same moment, his words stand, and both take effect.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question it just raised by pointing to a known מחלוקת in a similar case: one person who, in a single planned statement, says two things one after the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר says the first thing a person says is what counts. רבי יוסי says that if the person meant both from the start, we count both, because no one can say two words at once. Here the 'ratified, nullified' case is being compared to this, so according to רבי יוסי the הפרה can count too.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is bringing a source to answer a question
A substitute animal that gets the holiness of a קרבן

keyTerms.term: אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִקְרוֹת שְׁנֵי שֵׁמוֹת כְּאֶחָד
keyTerms.meaning: It is impossible to say two names at the same moment

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי יוסי says any two words count. He only counts both if the person meant both from the very beginning.

phrases.english: Come and hear from the dispute
of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei.
As we learned: 'This is hereby a substitute for a burnt-offering,
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in תמורה.

phrases.english: a substitute for a peace-offering'
it is a substitute for a burnt-offering only,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
And Rabbi Yosei says:
If this is what he intended from the start,
phrases.notes: He means: if he planned from the beginning for the animal to be a substitute for both.

phrases.english: since it is impossible to call it
two names at the same time,
his words stand.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע מִפְּלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבה's question from just before this, about saying 'ratified and nullified' while making the ratification depend on the nullification.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a הפרה said after a הקמה in one planned statement can take effect
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in תמורה: רבי מאיר versus רבי יוסי on 'a substitute for an עולה, a substitute for a שלמים'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Like רבי יוסי's view about a double תמורה, when the person planned both from the start, the second word (the הפרה) also takes effect, so the vow is nullified.

steps.title: Even רבי מאיר agrees in this case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds that רבי מאיר only follows the first word when the person did not tie the two together. Here the husband said the הקמה should not work unless the הפרה works, so even רבי מאיר agrees the הפרה takes effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even רבי מאיר only said his rule where the person did not say 'this one should not take effect unless that one takes effect.' But here, where he said 'the ratification should not take effect unless the nullification takes effect,' רבי מאיר also agrees that the nullification takes effect.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes the answer stronger: the הפרה works according to everyone, not only according to רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר follows the first word only when the person spoke plainly. Here the husband openly made the הקמה depend on the הפרה. So the הקמה cannot win alone, and the הפרה takes effect even for רבי מאיר.

keyTerms.meaning: Ratifying a vow, making it stand

steps.whatToRemember: If the husband says 'the ratification should not work unless the nullification works,' the הפרה takes effect, according to both רבי מאיר and רבי יוסי.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רבי מאיר's 'first word counts' rule is only about ordinary speech. A clear condition that ties the two together changes the result.

phrases.english: And even Rabbi Meir only said his rule
where he did not say: 'This should not take effect
unless this other one takes effect,'
but here, where he said:
'The ratification should not take effect
unless the nullification takes effect,'
Rabbi Meir also agrees
that the nullification takes effect.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Makes the proof from step 1 cover רבי מאיר's view as well.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: When the הקמה is made to depend on the הפרה, the הפרה takes effect according to everyone.

steps.title: Ratified and nullified at the same moment
steps.stepSummary: רבה asks what the law is if the husband says the vow is ratified and nullified at the very same moment.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה asked: if he says 'It is ratified and nullified for you' all at once, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה asks a new question: what happens if both are said as one single action, not one after the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier case the הקמה and the הפרה came in an order, even if both were planned. Here the husband wants them both to happen at the same instant. So the question is whether doing both at once changes anything.

keyTerms.meaning: At the same moment, all at once

phrases.english: Rabba asked:
'It is ratified and nullified for you'
at the same moment, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from an ordered, conditional statement to saying both at the same moment.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a הקמה and a הפרה said at the same instant have any effect?

steps.title: Answer from רבה's own rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers from רבה's own rule: anything that cannot work one after the other also cannot work when done at the same time.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear what רבה himself said: anything that cannot happen one after the other also cannot happen at the same moment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רבה's question using a general rule that רבה himself taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once a vow is ratified, it cannot be nullified afterward, so 'ratify, then nullify' does not work. רבה's rule says that if two things cannot work one after the other, they also cannot work together at the same moment. So when he says 'ratified and nullified' all at once, neither one takes effect.
steps.whatToRemember: רבה's rule: what cannot work one after the other cannot work at the same time either.

phrases.english: Come and hear, for Rabba said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל דָּבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּזֶה אַחַר זֶה,
phrases.english: Anything that does not work one after the other,
does not work even at the same moment.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Since ratifying and then nullifying does not work, ratifying and nullifying at the same time does not work either.

steps.title: Does 'ratified today' mean 'nullified tomorrow'?
steps.stepSummary: רבה asks about a husband who says 'It is ratified for you today.' Does that hint that tomorrow it will be nullified, or not, since he never said so?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה asked: if he says 'It is ratified for you today,' what is the law? Do we say it is as if he told her 'It is nullified for you tomorrow'? Or perhaps not, because he did not actually say that to her?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה opens a new question and gives the two ways to look at it. The discussion continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By saying 'today,' the husband seems to suggest the הקמה ends after today, which would sound like a הפרה tomorrow. On the other side, he never actually said the word 'nullified.' The question is whether a hint counts as a real הפרה.

phrases.english: Rabba asked:
'It is ratified for you today,' what is the law?
Do we say
that it is like one who said to her: 'It is nullified for you tomorrow,'

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא הָא לָא אֲמַר לַהּ?
phrases.english: or perhaps, he did not actually say that to her?
phrases.notes: He means: he never said the word 'nullified,' so maybe nothing was nullified.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question from רבה, still about how הקמה and הפרה work.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a הקמה limited to 'today' count as a הפרה for tomorrow, even though הפרה was never said?
